locations.name: DOWN STREET
locations.subtitle: Churchill's War Cabinet Bunker, 1939–1945
locations.body: Closed to passengers in 1932. Requisitioned by the Railway Executive Committee during the Blitz. Churchill held Cabinet meetings 60 feet below Mayfair while bombs fell above. The platform walls still bear wartime signage. Accessible via a ventilation shaft on Down Street, Mayfair.

locations.name: BROMPTON ROAD
locations.subtitle: WWII Anti-Aircraft Operations Centre
locations.body: Closed 1934. Deep below Knightsbridge, the station became the control centre for London's anti-aircraft gun batteries. Officers tracked Luftwaffe raids from the original ticket hall. The Ministry of Defence quietly sold it in 2014. A developer bought it for £53 million.

locations.name: ALDWYCH
locations.subtitle: Wartime Repository for the Elgin Marbles
locations.body: Opened 1907, closed 1994. During WWII the tunnels sheltered thousands of Londoners — and the Elgin Marbles from the British Museum, transported here by night. The station appears regularly in film productions. The platform clocks still run, maintained by the BBC.

locations.name: BRITISH MUSEUM
locations.subtitle: The Station That Never Opened
locations.body: Approved 1897. Built beneath Great Russell Street. Never opened to the public — deemed surplus when Holborn station opened nearby. The tunnels were used for military communications in both World Wars. In 1935, newspapers reported ghostly sightings of an Ancient Egyptian haunting the platforms. The station has never been publicly photographed.

locations.name: MOUNT PLEASANT MAIL RAIL
locations.subtitle: The Post Office's Secret Underground
locations.body: Operational 1927–2003. A driverless electric railway running 6.5 miles beneath central London, carrying 4 million letters per day at peak operation. Tunnels run directly beneath the Central line between Paddington and Whitechapel. Now a museum — but only 25% of the tunnels are open to visitors.

locations.name: KINGSWAY TRAM SUBWAY
locations.subtitle: London's Forgotten Underground Tram
locations.body: Opened 1906. A subterranean tram tunnel running beneath Kingsway between Aldwych and Theobald's Road. Extended in 1931 to accommodate double-deckers. Closed 1952. The tunnels became a flood relief sewer. A section near Waterloo Bridge was briefly used as a car park in the 1960s. The entrance at Southampton Row is sealed behind an ordinary office building.

locations.name: THAMES FLOOD BARRIER LINK
locations.subtitle: The Jubilee's Secret Defensive Design
locations.body: The Jubilee Line Extension (1999) was engineered with 11 flood-proof door systems capable of sealing the entire tunnel network within minutes of a Thames flood event. Each door weighs 15 tonnes. The system has never been fully deployed. Engineers tested it once, in 2007. Stratford station sits 12 metres below projected flood level.

locations.name: THE BRUNEL TUNNEL
locations.subtitle: First Underwater Railway Tunnel in the World, 1843
locations.body: Marc and Isambard Brunel spent 18 years building the Thames Tunnel between Wapping and Rotherhithe. Opened 1843 to pedestrians — the first tunnel under a navigable river anywhere on earth. Flooded twice during construction. Eleven workers died. It became part of the East London line in 1869 and is now used by the Overground. The original pedestrian shafts still exist.

locations.name: VAUXHALL CROSS TUNNELS
locations.subtitle: Rumoured MI6 Underground Connection
locations.body: The MI6 building at Vauxhall Cross (opened 1994) is widely reported to connect to the Victoria line platforms below. No official confirmation exists. Construction contractors noted unusual specifications in the Vauxhall station rebuild of the 1970s. Two unexplained ventilation structures on the Albert Embankment have no documented purpose. This record is unverified.

locations.name: GOODGE STREET DEEP SHELTER
locations.subtitle: Eisenhower's London HQ, 1944
locations.body: Built 1942, 100 feet below Goodge Street. One of eight deep-level shelters constructed beneath Central Line stations. Used by General Eisenhower as his London headquarters in the run-up to D-Day. The tunnels housed 8,000 bunks. Now used by a commercial document storage company. Access via a nondescript brick building on Tottenham Court Road.
